nameStory: Purple-stemmed angelica gets its name from its distinctive dark purple or reddish-purple stems that make it stand out among other plants. The 'angelica' part comes from medieval times, when people believed this plant had heavenly healing powers - so angelic that it could ward off evil spirits and cure ailments.
description: Purple-stemmed angelica is a tall, impressive wildflower that can tower over you at 4-8 feet high. It looks like a giant version of Queen Anne's lace, with large umbrella-shaped clusters of tiny white or greenish-white flowers sitting atop thick, hollow stems. The plant has large, compound leaves divided into many leaflets, giving it a lush, tropical appearance despite growing in northern climates. Its most striking feature is those telltale dark purple stems that make identification easy.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, hollow stems are deep purple to reddish-purple, smooth to the touch, and can be as thick as your thumb on mature plants

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large umbrella-shaped clusters (umbels) of tiny white or greenish-white flowers that smell sweet and attract many insects

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Huge compound leaves divided into many toothed leaflets, feeling slightly rough and smelling strongly aromatic when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Towering plant reaching 4-8 feet tall with a robust, sturdy appearance that dominates its surroundings

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, oval seeds with papery wings that turn brown and rattle in the dried flower heads by late summer

habitat: Look for purple-stemmed angelica in wet, rich soils along stream banks, river edges, and swampy woodlands throughout New England. It thrives in partially shaded areas with consistent moisture, often growing alongside skunk cabbage, jewelweed, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll find it from sea level up into the mountains, wherever there's flowing or standing water nearby.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the ground as thick, purple-tinged stems with tightly folded leaves beginning to unfurl.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the plant reaches full height and produces its impressive white flower umbels from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads that rattle in the wind, while leaves turn yellow before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to ground level, leaving only dried brown stems and seed heads that may persist.

funFact: Purple-stemmed angelica stems are completely hollow inside like natural drinking straws, and Indigenous peoples traditionally used them as pipe stems and even as straws for drinking - though modern foragers should never try this without expert guidance since the carrot family includes deadly poisonous look-alikes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with poison hemlock, which also has hollow stems but has white-spotted stems instead of solid purple ones. Remember: purple stems = angelica, spotted stems = stay away! Also much larger than Queen Anne's lace, which rarely exceeds 3 feet and has solid green stems.
contextualKnowledge: Purple-stemmed angelica belongs to the carrot family (Apiaceae), which includes many edible plants like carrots and parsley, but also some of the most deadly poisonous plants in North America. Never eat any plant in this family unless you're absolutely certain of identification, as the consequences of confusion can be fatal.
compareHints: Purple-stemmed angelica is much larger and more robust than its cousin sea-watch angelica, which grows in coastal salt marshes and has thicker, more succulent leaves. Wild angelica is not native to New England and is typically smaller with less intensely purple stems. Purple-stemmed angelica's massive size and deep purple coloring make it the most distinctive angelica in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sea-watch differs from purple-stemmed angelica by its coastal habitat, green (not purple) stems, and slightly more waxy, thick leaves adapted for salt tolerance.
Compared to its New England relatives, wild angelica has more consistently purple-colored stems than purple-stemmed angelica, which often shows purple only at the base or nodes.
